# The First Treaties

This fact sheet explains how the Treaty of Paris marked the first step towards European integration, and how the Treaties of Rome expanded its foundations through the creation of the European Communities. It highlights how these agreements fostered the idea of a common future while outlining the core objectives, main principles and institutional developments that emerged in the aftermath of the Second World War.

## Background

The disastrous effects of the Second World War and the constant threat of an East-West confrontation meant that Franco-German reconciliation became a top priority. The decision to pool the coal and steel industries of six founding Member States (Belgium, France, Germany, Italy, Luxembourg and the Netherlands) brought into force by the Treaty of Paris in 1951, marked the first step towards European integration. The Treaties of Rome of 1957 expanded the foundations of this integration, while further developing the Communities’ economic and institutional framework. 

## Legal basis

 Treaty establishing the European Coal and Steel Community (ECSC Treaty or Treaty of Paris): signed on 18 April 1951 and entered into force on 23 July 1952, this Treaty established the European Coal and Steel Community (ECSC) and set up common institutions, including the High Authority, Parliamentary Assembly, Council of Ministers, Court of Justice and a Consultative Committee. Article 97 provided for the expiry of the Treaty after 50 years, which took effect on 23 July 2002; 

 Treaties establishing the European Economic Community (EEC) and the European Atomic Energy Community (EAEC/Euratom), or the Treaties of Rome: signed on 25 March 1957 and entered into force on 1 January 1958, these Treaties established the European Economic Community (EEC) and the European Atomic Energy Community (Euratom). Article 240 of the EEC Treaty and Article 208 of the EAEC Treaty explicitly provided that both pacts were concluded for an unlimited period. 

## Objectives

 The founders of the ECSC were clear about their intentions for the Treaty, namely that it represented merely the first step towards a ‘European federation’. The common coal and steel market was to be an experiment which could gradually be extended to other economic spheres, culminating in a political Europe; 

 The aim of the EEC was to establish a common market based on the four freedoms of movement (goods, persons, capital and services); 

 The aim of Euratom was to coordinate the supply of fissile materials and the research programmes initiated or being prepared by Member States on the peaceful use of nuclear energy; 

 The preambles to the three Treaties reveal a unity of purpose behind the creation of the Communities, namely the conviction that the states of Europe must work together to build a common future, as this alone will enable them to control their destiny. 

## Main principles and developments of the European Communities

 A. Origins of European integration 

The European Communities (the ECSC, EEC and Euratom) were born of the desire for a united Europe, an idea which gradually took shape as a direct response to the events that had shattered the continent. In the wake of the Second World War, the strategic industries, in particular the steel industry, needed reorganising. The future of Europe, threatened by East-West confrontation, lay in Franco-German reconciliation.

The appeal made on 9 May 1950, by Robert Schuman, the French Foreign Minister, can be regarded as the starting point for European integration. At that time, the choice of coal and steel was highly symbolic: in the early 1950s, coal and steel were vital industries and the basis of a country’s power. In addition to the clear economic benefits, the pooling of French and German resources was intended to mark the end of the rivalry between the two countries. On 9 May 1950, Robert Schuman declared: ‘Europe will not be made all at once, or according to a single plan. It will be built through concrete achievements which first create a de facto solidarity.’ It was on the basis of this principle that France, Italy, Germany and the Benelux countries (Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg) signed the Treaty of Paris, which concentrated predominantly on ensuring:

 free movement of goods and free access to sources of production; 

 permanent monitoring of the market to avoid distortions which could lead to the introduction of production quotas; 

 compliance with the rules of competition and the principle of price transparency; 

 support for modernisation and conversion of the coal and steel sectors. 

 B. From the EDC to the Treaties of Rome 

Following the signing of the Treaty of Paris, and despite France being opposed to the re-establishment of a German national military force, René Pleven proposed the formation of a European army. This led to the 1952 negotiation of the European Defence Community (EDC), which was intended to be accompanied by a Political Community (EPC). However, both plans were shelved following the French National Assembly’s refusal to ratify the treaty on 30 August 1954.

Efforts to relaunch the process of European integration following the failure of the EDC took the form of specific proposals at the Messina Conference in June 1955 on a customs union and atomic energy. These culminated in the signing of the EEC and EAEC Treaties.

 C. The common market and common policies 

The Treaty establishing the European Economic Community (EEC Treaty, the Treaty of Rome) included provisions on:

 eliminating customs duties between Member States; 

 establishing an external Common Customs Tariff; 

 introducing common policies for agriculture and transport; 

 creating a European Social Fund; 

 establishing a European Investment Bank; 

 developing closer relations between the Member States. 

To achieve these objectives the EEC Treaty laid down guiding principles and established the framework for the legislative activities of the Community institutions. These included common policies, such as : the common agricultural policy (Articles 38 to 43), transport policy (Articles 74 and 75) and a common commercial policy (Articles 110 to 113). The common market was intended to guarantee the free movement of goods and the mobility of factors of production, including the free movement of workers and enterprises, the freedom to provide services and the free movement of capital.

The Treaty establishing the European Atomic Energy Community (Euratom Treaty) originally set highly ambitious objectives, including the speedy establishment and growth of nuclear industries. However, owing to the complex and sensitive nature of the nuclear sector, which touched on the vital interests of the Member States (defence and national independence), those ambitions had to be scaled back.

 D. Institutional development of the Communities 

The Convention on certain institutions common to the European Communities, which was signed and entered into force at the same time as the Treaties of Rome, stipulated that the Parliamentary Assembly and Court of Justice would be common institutions. The process of institutional unification was completed by the Treaty establishing a Single Council and a Single Commission of the European Communities of 8 April 1965, known as the Merger Treaty.

From that point onwards, the EEC held sway over the sectoral communities, the ECSC and the EAEC. This marked the triumph of the general EEC system over the coexistence of organisations with sectoral competence, and the establishment of its institutions.

## Role of the European Parliament

The Treaty of Paris established a Common Assembly as one of the institutions of the ECSC. The Convention on certain institutions common to the European Communities, signed alongside the Treaties of Rome, further provided for a common Parliamentary Assembly and Court of Justice for the Communities, which contributed to the gradual unification of the institutional framework of the European Communities.
